items.title: “What Makes It Alright to Dig Up Our Ancestral Remains?”: An Interview With Carmen Lucas, Kwaaymii Laguna Band of Indians

extra.summary: ABSTRACT Carmen Lucas is a tribal monitor, expert, and elder of the Kwaaymii Laguna Band of Indians, San Diego County, California. She learned about cultural landscapes and Ancestral human remains from her father, the late Tom Lucas—the last full‐blooded descendant of the Kwaaymii—and has been a caretaker of the Kwaaymii Homeland and burial grounds at the former Laguna Indian Reservation for the last 50 years. After a 20 year career in the United States Marine Corps, Lucas has worked in the field of cultural resource management (CRM) as a tribal monitor, consultant, and educator. She has helped archaeologists and tribal monitors to identify archaeological deposits, Ancestral remains, and burial items to promote avoidance and preservation in place. Lucas also serves on the State of California's Truth & Healing Council as a voting member. Along with historians, archaeologists, and her attorney Courtney Ann Coyle, Lucas has helped to write and successfully nominate at least five historic properties to the National Register of Historic Places based on their tribal cultural values. In this interview, Lucas provides critical insights on the role of anthropology and archaeology in CRM, especially as it relates to the development of renewable energy and mineral extraction.

extra.summary: ABSTRACT This article critically examines INDIAsize—an Indian government–funded anthropometric initiative to “decolonize” body size standards used in clothing production. Drawing on ethnographic fieldwork conducted in New Delhi between 2020 and 2024, I demonstrate how body size research and design standards–making processes become sites for negotiating ideologies of citizenship and belonging in postcolonial contexts. The analysis extends anthropological scholarship on consumer movements by theorizing how contemporary designers deploy body standards, scientific authority, enumeration, and classification to police ethnic boundaries within consumer capitalism. I develop the concept of “embodied citizenship” to characterize these political struggles over the tangible, material, and epistemic conditions of corporeal access through which worldly participation is lived, contested, and claimed. items.title: When Humans Need Gods and Gods Need Humans: Prophetic Authority and Ritual Negotiation in Himachal Pradesh

extra.summary: ABSTRACT In Himachal Pradesh, India, village deities act as political figures who play an active role in communal affairs, especially during periods of social change. Bakhan , an annual divination ritual in which these deities speak through human mediums, is a public event that offers forecasts and instructions. I argue that the bakhan is a social arena in which divine authority is publicly enacted and made answerable to communal judgment. Drawing on ethnographic research, I develop the concept of “performative accountability” to show how prophetic claims gain force through a process in which they are voiced, interpreted, increasingly questioned, and measured against subsequent events. Divine authority, I argue, does not rest on revelation alone but takes shape through ongoing relations of recognition and response between gods and villagers. The bakhan reveals a form of authority sustained through public scrutiny rather than being insulated from it.

items.title: AI Ethics, US Militarism, and World Crises
items.affiliation: Lancaster University; Hong Kong Polytechnic University; University of Washington

extra.summary: ABSTRACT Lucy Suchman, professor emerita at Lancaster University, UK, is a foundational figure in human‐computer interaction and a leading critical voice on artificial intelligence. Suchman's research works at the intersections of anthropology and the field of feminist science and technology studies, focused on the sociotechnical imaginaries, material practices, and politics of technology design. Her current research extends her longstanding critical engagement with AI to the domain of contemporary militarism. Suchman is a graduate of the University of California, Berkeley, obtaining her BA in 1972, MA in 1977, and doctorate in social and cultural anthropology in 1984. Before coming to Lancaster, Suchman worked for 22 years at Xerox's Palo Alto Research Center (PARC) in California, where she held the positions of principal scientist and manager of the Work Practice and Technology research group. Our interview was conducted in the midst of multiple, intersecting crises, as people in different parts of the world face profound uncertainties brought about by geopolitical tensions, warfare, economic instability, and rapid technological developments. Situating the question of AI within these broader contexts, especially the evolving US militarism, this interview examines AI ethics in light of the political, economic, and technological conditions shaping contemporary life worldwide.

extra.summary: Abstract Above the banana plantations of northern Martinique, drones and satellites read the surface of the land for the stress it endures and the yield it promises. Beneath them, in soil that a synthetic pesticide has saturated for centuries to come, the ground is quietly undoing what was done to it. This lecture gives that undoing two names. The first is terrestrial knowledge , or what the ground knows: the biological intelligence that plants, insects, and microbes produce as they adapt, at temporal scales no algorithm can apprehend. The second is vegetality , or how the ground knows, and how it lives, endures, and keeps time. Drawing on more than a decade of fieldwork in Martinique, where the pesticide chlordécone lingers in the soil, the lecture follows the responses of organisms inhabiting toxic ground and argues that the plantation and the digital platform are genealogically continuous: inheritors of a single extractive grammar, both blind to what the ground does in response.

items.title: A new paradigm in the American Anthropological Association

extra.summary: Is the most critical issue facing anthropology departments their whiteness? In an address to the American Anthropological Association, then-president Akhil Gupta announced a “racial reckoning” and “decolonizing project.” Whiteness, white space, or white-norming is how liberal antiracist anthropology continues to harbor racism, Gupta and other critical theorists hold. They further argue that the racial and political identity of anthropologists—either as voices of marginalized groups or allies of such groups—should determine the future of our field. This is a new paradigm, I argue, and my term for it is Neo-Racial Anthropology. Neo-racialism grows out of increasing skepticism about the value of crossing sociocultural divides to do ethnographic research. Ethnographic research also has been undermined by the presumed moral authority of the oppressed. Once neo-racialists add the assumption that white hegemony is the key underlying issue in most situations, an anthropologist’s racial identity becomes a key determinant of what they judge to be the best new research. This is the logic that turns neo-racialists into racial reductionists. If other anthropologists acquiesce to this kind of thinking, an ethnography-based interpretive social science could ossify into an academic priesthood.

items.title: Concerning the boundaries of serious anthropology, or: Can witches fly?

extra.summary: In a commentary on German anthropology in the 1970s and 1980s, the literary critic Peter Braun has remarked that Duerr’s essay “Can witches fly?” (together with Hubert Fichte’s “Heretical remarks for a new human sciences”) represented nothing less than a charter “for the revolutionary renewal of anthropology against the orthodox forces of the discipline” (Braun 2002: 223). As the literary critic Ian Robinson once observed (1975: 124), “‘In reality’ is the assertion that one set of rules should judge the rest, especially if they are the rules of physics.” Duerr’s compact and sometimes cryptic argument is essentially an exploration of how such judgments about reality are made with respect to claims of sorcerous flight, from the Renaissance scholar Della Porta to the ethnographer Carlos Castaneda. How is an anthropologist to get to grips with such experiences? It cannot be, suggests Duerr, by positing that alien forms of life are radically incomparable, nor yet by assuming that they can be neatly folded into our own frameworks. Instead, we ought to keep ourselves open to the onto-epistemic surprises occasioned by boundary crossings and borderline cases. For if—as Duerr suggests elsewhere (1985a: 131)—“shocks are the precondition for insight” then this is only so long as we allow ourselves the possibility of being affected.

items.title: Fighting the system, saving the Earth

extra.summary: This article shows how the environmental crisis is understood and conceptualized within the Czech conspiritual milieu. It attends to the so-called conspiracy theories, seeing them as a form of knowledge, which is assembled as people develop sensibility to affects, atmospheres, and resonances. This shift in perception allows the self-styled “Awakened” to perceive an upcoming Collapse, a disaster that also bears a promise of a radical social transformation. To some degree this notion of Collapse overlaps with concerns about climate change but is primarily understood as a moral and spiritual problem that needs to be addressed—by caring for the Earth and accepting truth claims about the conspiratorial nature of the world. This position makes certain modes of political action open, while closing others.

items.title: In the witches’ kitchen

extra.summary: An introduction to Hans Peter Duerr’s severely neglected classic , Dreamtime (1978) 1985b . German anthropology is finally receiving much-needed attention; hence, the present work is partly intended as a contribution to these ongoing efforts to explicate it for an Anglophone audience. But more than this, Dreamtime ’s challenging argument critically engages with themes of major importance to contemporary anthropology more generally—among them, the interrelated issues of ontology, translation, and transformation. I attempt to explore this and trace out the significant affinities and resonances of Duerr’s argument with the work of an eclectic collective of others, including Evans-Pritchard, William James, Sahlins, Stengers, and Deleuze.

items.title: Mammoth 2.0

extra.summary: Based on multi-sited ethnographic fieldwork conducted in the Russian Arctic and the United States, this article examines de-extinction—the technoscientific effort to recreate extinct species through genetic engineering. Focusing on attempts to create the so-called Arctic elephant, I follow preserved mammoth tissue, shifting scientific narratives, and flows of capital across cryogenic storage sites, biotech labs, and Arctic landscapes. These trajectories reveal how de-extinction goes beyond its aim to “reverse” extinction, reworking time itself as an experimental material. Cryopreservation halts decay; cellular reprogramming resets cells to an earlier state; genome editing reconstructs evolutionary sequences. In this process, time becomes not a backdrop to life but something open to redesign—manipulated, modified, suspended, or simply taken off the table. De-extinction projects treat extinction as an interval rather than an end, transforming biological past into a platform for speculative engineering. The article contributes to anthropological debates on death, time, and technoscientific imagination.

items.title: How did borders get so bad?

extra.summary: Recent anthropology theorizes borders primarily as technologies of exclusion that perpetuate structural inequality and racialized violence. This perspective downplays the varied cultural meanings of boundaries that shape identities within and amongst countries of the global south, ultimately resting on a neo-functionalist model of borders and boundary-making. Using the shifting politics of boundaries between Honduras and El Salvador as an example, this article shows how historical boundary-making practices affect contemporary Central American migratory patterns, with a specific focus on the position of Salvadoran migrants in Honduras. Ultimately, I reassert the importance of a meaning-centered analysis of borders as an alternative to neo-functionalism.

items.title: Obstinate truths

extra.summary: This article examines a central epistemological dilemma of the post-truth moment: how anthropology can remain committed to grounding knowledge in vernacular meaning-making when everyday understandings of the world increasingly draw on exclusionary ideas. Reflecting on unsettling theories about climate change and the environment encountered in my home village in the southern Austrian Alps, an area affected by rapid ecological change, I explore what happens when ethnographic attention reaches the outer edges of anthropological knowledge production. Drawing on Alf Lüdtke and Antonio Gramsci—two theorists who probed such edges from within their own historical conjunctures—I argue that taking seriously eigensinnige (obstinate) modes of everyday sense-making about environmental change offers a crucial analytical opening. Attending to these antagonistic truth claims not only illuminates the fraught relationship between vernacular and normative forms of knowledge-making but also compels us to rethink the nature of the everyday itself.

items.title: Red-pilled

extra.summary: This article contributes to anthropological scholarship on the politics of (post-)truth by linking anthropology’s legacy of epistemic contingency to the memetic truth practices of far-right digital culture. Drawing on fourteen months of digital ethnography among German far-right activists on Discord, 4chan, Twitch, and X (2021–2023), I analyze “red-pill stories” as performances of truthiness—affective narratives of awakening that consolidate community through stickiness rather than factual verification. Reading these stories as “deep stories” in Hochschild’s sense, I show that red-pilling is a form of secondary enculturation. In the second part of the article, I use my field encounters with a would-be red-piller as a lens to examine how far-right actors exploit anthropological concepts—epistemic contingency, partial truths, ontological difference—to demand legitimacy, thereby forcing anthropologists to confront the unruly heritage of their own epistemology.

items.title: Surprises in a minor key

extra.summary: What are the epistemological strategies of anthropology as a globally decentered discipline? How do anthropologists work beyond the colonially inflected geopolitics of surprise, in which knowledge supposedly emerges from a serendipitous encounter between the modern Western liberal subject and the non-modern Other? Ethnologists and anthropologists working in regions with historical experiences of socialist modernity have engaged with different modalities of surprise, only some of which have been theorized as relevant to disciplinary epistemology. Thinking through surprises in a minor key and drawing on the epistemological traditions of European ethnology, I suggest that conducting ethnology and anthropology in post/socialist modernities can be understood as a study of the unexpected in everyday life.

items.title: When silence speaks

extra.summary: Drawing on fieldwork in Istanbul, this article explores the practices of silencing characterizing relationships between parents and children in Turkish leftist families affected by state violence in the wake of the 1980 coup. It shows how silence and secrecy can be understood as a set of embodied experiences and reflective actions that are intersubjective and which convey emotions, values, and a tacit knowledge of the state. Moving beyond the trauma paradigm, such practices are interpreted as a field of meaning-making through which political cultures, generational boundaries, and collective representations are produced and negotiated. Likewise, former revolutionaries’ habit of silencing personal memories in favor of we-centered narratives is seen not as a sign of traumatic unspeakability or political oppression, but as a collective process of intimate selving through which they reconstruct their revolutionary moral economy in the present.

items.title: On researching “pseudolaw” in sovereignist movements

extra.summary: The so-called “conspiratorial sovereignism” milieu in Germany is made up of groups that contest the authority of the state through ritualized interactions inspired by conspiratorial legal claims. Drawing on one year of ethnographic fieldwork and online observation, I analyze how these groups enact alternative sovereignties and legalities. Analytically separating the different ways in which states can be understood as fantasies through the dimensions of the imagined, imaginary, and un/acceptable, I suggest that anthropological frameworks that view the state as a social fantasy provide important insights into these performances, but risk normalizing and romanticizing the movement’s deeply hierarchical and exclusionary ideologies. The article calls for critical reflection on implicit normative biases in the scholarship, emphasizing the need to understand sovereignism’s political dangers beyond hegemonic/marginal divides.

items.title: When is hoarding?

extra.summary: This article reconsiders hoarding not as a psychological disorder, but as a phenomenon embedded in the temporality of social life. Drawing on ethnographic research in Japan, it explores local understandings of accumulation and disorder in three contexts: the biographical trajectories of participants, the everyday rhythms of consumption and disposal, and the material temporalities that emerge when objects are taken out of circulation. Rather than describing hoarding disorder as an enduring mental health condition, the article shows how domestic accumulations become salient at moments of biographical transition, specifically marriage and/or cohabitation. The contrasting experiences of women and men reveal how domestic accumulations become problematic when they disrupt culturally normative trajectories of household formation and family life. Interviews with participants also reveal systemic barriers to disposal, such as rigid waste collection schedules that privilege middle-class norms, making accumulation a social, not merely personal, deviance. Finally, accumulated objects acquire significance through their temporal suspension outside ordinary circulation, becoming indeterminate things whose meanings are resolved only through later acts of sorting and disposal. Taken together, these findings suggest an alternative understanding of hoarding that traces a path through the thicket of the social field rather than the internal landscape of the psyche.

items.title: Awkward alignments
items.affiliation: University of Cologne; Martin Luther University Halle-Wittenberg

extra.summary: Anthropological knowledge is increasingly contested in our postliberal world, both from within and outside the discipline. Against this backdrop, this article addresses two interrelated questions: first, how should we methodologically address this challenge of contested anthropological knowledge-making and, second, what should be anthropology’s political approach in the (post-)truth era? We argue that anthropology best handles these conundrums through a research orientation we describe as aiming for “awkward alignments.” In awkward alignments, anthropologists engage their interlocutors with an ethico-onto-epistemological attitude of “empathetic skepticism,” attempting to understand how people think and act on the basis of their own experiences with similar situations while at the same time systematically questioning all knowledge claims. While suggesting that anthropologists should practice empathetic skepticism across the full spectrum of their research encounters, they should simultaneously not shy away, politically, from an “agonistic confrontation” when engaging “normative others” during and beyond their research.

items.title: The politics of (post-)truth
items.affiliation: Johannes Gutenberg University Mainz; Martin Luther University Halle-Wittenberg

extra.summary: The introduction to this special section explores the contemporary politics of (post-)truth as both an object of anthropological inquiry and a challenge to anthropological knowledge-making itself. Rather than treating post-truth as a simple erosion of facts, we examine how contemporary conflicts increasingly concern the conditions under which truth claims are validated, contested, and rendered authoritative. Drawing on debates in anthropology, science and technology studies, and post-positivist scholarship, we revisit long-standing concerns with epistemic plurality, incommensurability, collaboration, and the social production of knowledge. We argue that the current conjuncture is marked less by the existence of competing truths than by intensified struggles over the infrastructures, procedures, and normative frameworks that make truth claims intelligible and actionable. Introducing the contributions to this special section, we propose the concepts of “good-enough truths” and “minimal commensurability” as analytical tools for navigating tensions between epistemic openness, normative accountability, and democratic contestation under increasingly polarized conditions.

items.title: Walking the tightrope

extra.summary: This article examines the ethical and methodological challenges and possibilities of conducting public ethnography and studying far-right voters in precarious settings. Drawing on twenty-six years of longitudinal research in Brazil, I reflect on how long-standing relationships with interlocutors—many of whom have adopted authoritarian views over time—can be sustained amid deep political disagreement and contested truths. As a public scholar, I examine how visibility and transparency have reshaped both the ethnographic encounter and ethnographic authority, making politics an unavoidable dimension of fieldwork. The analysis foregrounds the emotional and political tightrope walked by ethnographers who must balance empathy, nuance, and critique. The paper shows how mutual interests, long-term trust, and agonistic intimacy make it possible to build understanding without endorsement. Ultimately, I argue that public ethnography and studying ideological opponents produce an irresolvable contradiction best met through transparency, reflexive limits, and an acceptance of coeval change and contested truths.

items.title: Beyond orthodoxies of race and class: introduction
items.affiliation: Loyola Marymount University; Drake University; West Virginia University

extra.summary: Race and class have long been contested and pitted against one another within scholarship and social justice struggles. This introduction to the special issue Beyond Orthodoxies of Race and Class maps the theoretical terrain of these debates rather than adjudicating which orthodoxies must be transcended. Situating race-class inquiry within decades of left retreat and an intensifying far-right politics, it traces divides among class-centered, race-centered, and intersectional approaches, alongside bridging traditions including racial capitalism, decolonial theory, Black internationalism, Indigenous political economy, caste studies, and a critical theory of racism. The editors argue that both class-blind race analysis and race-blind class analysis yield flawed political strategies, as racism and capitalism are mutually constitutive. The thirteen contributions, organized around race-class contestation, history, epistemology, Indigeneity and caste, and education and community, reflect divergent positions. The issue is offered as an invitation to dialogue across theoretical traditions, in service of effective emancipatory analysis and organizing.

items.title: Race, class and totality: left disputes over how to think and know

extra.summary: This article engages with several of the contributed chapters in On Class, Race, and Educational Reform (Darder, A., C. Hayes II, and H. Ryan. eds. [2023. On Class, Race, and Educational Reform: Contested Perspectives. London: Bloomsbury]) to explore deeper issues in political and social theory that undergird the left’s longstanding race-class debate. These include conflicting beliefs about grand theory, particularity versus totality, categorical primacy among social systems and “oppressions”, and epistemology. The pertinent contested frameworks are Marxism, critical race theory, intersectionality, decoloniality and postmodernism/poststructuralism. Race-class debate has conventionally tangled over competing primacies, and such queries should indeed continue. The article, however, seeks to plow deeper, to examine certain competing assumptions and ways of knowing that may impede left discussion – on race, class and more.

items.title: Contradictory intersections of class and race in settler colonial societies

extra.summary: Consideration of the social positions and experiences of Indigenous people within settler colonial societies poses challenges to conventional understandings of race and class. Indigenous peoples, displaced and marginalized through the development of colonial structures, have also demonstrated remarkable resiliency, contributing in significant ways to the development of settler societies. While they often share similar positions and circumstances with other minoritized groups based on class and racial factors, they are distinguished by their longstanding relationships with lands and waters, their encounters with colonization, and their rights and status as Indigenous or first peoples. This article, focusing on the Canadian context, explores the implications that these Indigenous experiences hold for understanding the intersections among capitalist relations and colonialism, in conjunction with the emergence of and struggles against contemporary systems of inequality and oppression.

items.title: Anti‐Colonial Colonialism: Imperialist Identities of Russia and China in Their Quest for Post‐Subalternity

extra.summary: ABSTRACT Why do Russia and China legitimize colonial and imperial practices through anti‐colonial and anti‐Western rhetoric? This article compares how both regimes discursively justify coercive policies toward culturally proximate Others (Ukrainians, Taiwanese, Hongkongers) and culturally alien Others (Crimean Tatars, Uyghurs, Tibetans). It argues that colonialism is legitimized as a means of reaffirming supranational imperialist identities to pursue post‐subalternity reconstituting itself as an autonomous centre of a hierarchical order with own civilizational model as an alternative to dominant Western norms. Through processes of othering and blame‐shifting, Russia and China portray targeted populations as victims or proxies of Western neo‐colonial manipulation, framing their own domination as protective, defensive and emancipatory. This strategy, conceptualized as ‘anti‐colonial colonization’, allows both states to depict repression, assimilation and military aggression as morally necessary acts of decolonization. Drawing on discursive analysis of official and semi‐official sources, the article shows how identity‐driven colonialism legitimizes violence at home and abroad.

items.title: Re‐Signifying Soviet Monuments: State Self‐Description, Memory Politics and Ontological Security in Estonia

extra.summary: ABSTRACT Since the restoration of independence, Soviet‐era monuments in Estonia have remained contested sites through which historical legitimacy, political belonging and national identity are publicly negotiated. Following Russia's full‐scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022, these monuments acquired renewed salience as Estonia moved to regulate symbols that had become flashpoints in struggles over memory and the symbolic order of the nation‐state. This article examines how Soviet monuments in Estonia are re‐signified. Drawing on a data‐driven typology‐building approach and an analytical reconstruction of salient interventions since 1991, it develops a fourfold typology of re‐signification strategies and identifies the conditions under which they de‐escalate contestation, intensify it or displace it onto other symbolic sites and issues. The article shows how semiotic mechanisms of state self‐description shape these processes and argues that monument re‐signification is central to the symbolic reproduction of political community under conditions of ontological insecurity.

items.title: Modernisation, Migration and National Identification: Evidence From Central Asia

extra.summary: ABSTRACT Under which conditions do individuals identify as citizens of a state? This paper addresses this question in the context of four Central Asia states (Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan, Tajikistan and Uzbekistan) using seven waves of Central Asia Barometer Survey Data. Despite concerns that particularistic attachments undermine nation‐building in the region, a clear majority of respondents in each country identify as citizens. Employing multilevel statistical models, the analysis tests hypotheses derived from modernisation theory and exchange‐theoretic approaches and also examines the role of group‐level structural factors. The results provide general support for modernisation‐based expectations, while also revealing a distinctive regional pattern in which rural residents are more likely than urban residents to identify as citizens. Most importantly, the findings demonstrate that transnational labour migration weakens national identification: reliance on remittances is consistently associated with a lower probability of identifying as a citizen. This result highlights a structural tension facing remittance‐dependent states, in which economic reliance on external labour markets may weaken national attachment.

items.title: What can linguistic justice researchers and practitioners learn from more than a century of social justice debates?

extra.summary: The concept of linguistic justice is increasingly understood by researchers and practitioners as being linked to, or part of, social justice. However, social justice itself is a contested concept that has changed definition over time, and which takes numerous, sometimes incommensurable, forms today. This article thus aims to support linguistic justice researchers and practitioners to understand and clarify how they conceptualize social justice. To do this, I provide a brief cross-disciplinary overview of major debates surrounding the concept of social justice, starting from the terms’ first appearance in the nineteenth century. In doing so I explore three significant forms of social justice from the nineteenth to the twenty-first centuries: reactionary justice, global justice, and decolonial justice. I then examine the implications that these different approaches have for how we theorize and pursue linguistic justice. In doing so, this article aims to provide bibliographic, terminological, and conceptual resources for anyone wishing to develop a more robust and transparent approach to linking social justice and linguistic justice in their work.

items.title: Linguistic distance and first migration destination choice among rural migrants in China
items.source: Journal of Ethnic and Migration Studies

extra.summary: Regional linguistic differences may form informal boundaries in internal migration, yet their role in destination choice remains underexplored. This study examines linguistic distance as an origin–destination relational attribute in first migration destination choice among rural migrants in China. Using the China Migrants Dynamic Survey, the analysis matches first-migration information for 31,464 rural workers with city-level data, yielding 4,636,771 individual–alternative-city observations. Linguistic distance is constructed from the hierarchical structure of Chinese dialects and five minority languages using 2010 county-level registered-population weights. Conditional logit estimates show a significant negative association between linguistic distance and destination choice. The full-model odds ratio is 0.7901, indicating that a one-unit increase in linguistic distance is associated with a 20.99% reduction in relative odds. This association persists across alternative linguistic-distance measures, choice sets, sample restrictions and additional controls. The interaction between income disparity and linguistic distance is significantly negative, while the negative association with linguistic distance is weaker among new-generation migrants. These findings highlight linguistic boundaries within countries and show how linguistic relationships, economic disparities and migrant heterogeneity jointly inform internal migration destination choice.

items.title: The redefined Naga: from colonial entrancement to digital disruption

extra.summary: This article examines how digital platforms are reshaping Naga identity by transforming Indigenous self-representation, cultural transmission, and social authority. Colonial administration and Christian missionary intervention disrupted village institutions, imposed homogenising ethnic categories, and produced legacies that continue to shape contemporary inequalities. The study draws on ethnographic fieldwork, in-depth interviews, and digital ethnography to conceptualise digital platforms as ‘digital Morungs’: vernacular spaces for cultural transmission, entrepreneurship, political engagement, and identity-making. The findings show that digital Morungs enable Nagas to reclaim narratives, build affective publics, and connect with wider Indigenous networks while simultaneously reproducing infrastructural inequalities, linguistic hierarchies, and algorithmically mediated forms of visibility that privilege individual self-branding over communal values. The article argues that digital participation simultaneously decolonises representation and reconfigures historical inequalities through platform logics, contributing to debates on digital indigeneity, platformisation, and Indigenous digital futures.

items.title: Between Modernisation and Inequality: Semarang-Cirebon Railway Line Operation in the Dutch Colonial Period, 1895–1910
items.source: KEMANUSIAAN the Asian Journal of Humanities
items.affiliation: Diponegoro University; National Research and Innovation Agency

extra.summary: This study examined the modernisation efforts of the Dutch East Indies colonial government through the operation of the Semarang-Cirebon railway line under the Semarang-Cheribon Stoomtram Maatschappij (SCS) from 1895 until 1910. The method used was the historical method with the socioeconomic approach. This study found that the construction of the Semarang-Cirebon railway line was driven by the capitalist trend of the time, which spurred the rapid growth of plantation businesses along the line, thereby increasing the need for adequate transportation. Although the railway significantly influenced the development of the plantation sector, its presence created new problems. The decline in community food production due to the large-scale clearing of plantation land throughout the Semarang-Cirebon area encouraged import policies that actually triggered famine and disease. On the other hand, some of SCS’s actions seemed discriminatory and exploitative, such as the imposition of passenger fares based on population groups and the company’s enormous revenues that, in fact, never improved welfare, especially for indigenous people, sharpening inequality among the population. This study concludes that the modernisation efforts carried out by the colonialists through the Semarang-Cirebon railway line were a subtle strategy to strengthen their power and obtain maximum profits in the colony.

items.title: Exploring the relationship between cultural landscapes and psychological well-being through indigenous environmental design in rural China
items.affiliation: Shanxi University of Finance and Economics; Shanghai Urban Construction Vocational College

extra.summary: Introduction Indigenous environmental design in rural China is increasingly affected by modernization, tourism development, and ecological change. However, empirical evidence concerning the relationship between cultural landscape fidelity and residents’ psychological well-being remains limited. This study developed the Cultural Landscape–Psychological Well-being (CL-PWB) Nexus Model to examine the association between Indigenous Environmental Design Fidelity (IEDF) and psychological well-being, considering place attachment, perceived restorativeness, and cultural identity continuity as mediators, and ritual-spatial synchrony (RSS) and social cohesion (SC) as potential moderators. Methods A sequential explanatory mixed-methods design was employed. The quantitative phase involved a cross-sectional survey of 420 residents from four ethnic minority villages in rural China. Confirmatory factor analysis and regression-based moderated mediation analysis with bootstrapped confidence intervals were used to examine the proposed relationships. The qualitative phase comprised thematic analysis of 40 in-depth and key-informant interviews to contextualise and complement the quantitative findings. Results IEDF was positively associated with psychological well-being. This association was statistically accounted for by place attachment, perceived restorativeness, and cultural identity continuity, with the direct association becoming non-significant after the mediators were included. items.title: Narrative ‘Self-Grasping’ and Ontological Insecurity: Beijing’s Sinicisation of Tibetan and Uyghur Histories

extra.summary: This article interrogates the Chinese state’s pursuit of ontological security (OS) through the Sinicisation of history, conceptualised as narrative self-grasping. Drawing on Buddhist philosophy and ontological security theory, it argues that China’s quest to achieve existential stability by constructing a coherent, teleological national self – the Zhonghua minzu – paradoxically generates deeper existential insecurity. Through an analysis of Chinese historiography and Tibetan and Uyghur counter-narratives, the article demonstrates how the state’s effort to dissolve historical plurality into a singular story of national identity provokes narrative resistance. Tibetan narratives of sacred descent and distinctive history and identity, and Uyghur historiographies of endurance and moral remembrance collectively expose the fragility of the state’s existential project. By juxtaposing the state’s narrative totalisation with Buddhist critiques of attachment to illusory identity, the study reconceptualises OS as the capacity to dwell with narrative contingency rather than real ising, mastering or denying it. The article thus advances an alternative understanding of security grounded in ontological humility and plural coexistence, revealing that the more the state narrates itself into permanence, the more unstable its being becomes .

items.title: Spatial patterns and environmental suitability of traditional Tibetan villages in Ganzi Tibetan Autonomous Prefecture, China
items.affiliation: Sichuan Provincial Architectural Design and Research Institute (China); Sichuan University; Hubei University for Nationalities

extra.summary: The acceleration of global urbanization and industrialization since the 20th century has drawn increasing attention to the quality of human settlements. Ganzi Tibetan Autonomous Prefecture, located on the southeastern Tibetan Plateau, is characterized by rugged terrain, fragile ecosystems, and cultural diversity. Its traditional villages exhibit strong adaptation to local environmental conditions in site selection, spatial configuration, and construction practices; however, rapid modernization and environmental change have increasingly affected their spatial distribution and living conditions. In this study, 274 traditional villages listed by the Ministry of Housing and Urban-Rural Development and the Sichuan Provincial Government were selected as research samples. An integrated framework combining spatial pattern analysis, environmental suitability assessment, and factor detection analysis was applied. ArcGIS spatial analysis, multi-index evaluation, and the GeoDetector model were employed to examine spatial distribution patterns, environmental suitability, and associated factors. The results indicate that traditional villages in Ganzi are significantly clustered, forming a “two cores–multiple scattered points” pattern, primarily concentrated in Danba and Litang. Clear inter-county disparities are observed, showing a general “south-dense and north-sparse” tendency. items.title: Stakeholder-Oriented Ecotourism Management and Marketing: A Sustainability Performance Evaluation of Chengyang Eight Villages in Guangxi, China

extra.summary: As ecotourism destinations face increasing market competition and growing sustainability pressures, destination managers must balance stakeholder interests while converting ecological, sociocultural, and economic resources into sustainable market value. Drawing on stakeholder theory, strategic management, and destination marketing perspectives, this study develops a stakeholder-oriented sustainability performance evaluation framework for ecotourism management. Fourteen indicators across economic, sociocultural, and environmental dimensions are constructed through a literature review and evaluated from the perspective of indigenous residents as core stakeholders. Using the Analytic Hierarchy Process (AHP), Likert-scale survey data, and Chengyang Eight Villages in Guangxi, China as the empirical setting, the study assesses the relative managerial priorities of sustainable ecotourism development. The reported dimension weights assign the highest priority to economic sustainability, followed by sociocultural sustainability, whereas environmental sustainability receives the lowest relative weight. items.title: Developing a Culturally Responsive Mental Health Support Guide for First-Year University Students in Yunnan, China: A Mixed-Methods Formative Evaluation
items.source: Journal of College Student Mental Health
items.affiliation: King Mongkut's Institute of Technology Ladkrabang

extra.summary: This mixed-methods developmental study developed and formatively evaluated a culturally responsive mental health support guide for first-year university students experiencing adjustment-related depressive distress in Yunnan, China. Designed as a low-threshold, non-diagnostic resource, the guide supports early recognition, psychoeducation, guided reflection, basic coping practice, and referral awareness. Its preliminary version comprised four modules – Growing, Retracting, Healing, and Combating – with 20 sub-guidelines and 79 strategy items. Content adequacy and usability were evaluated through quantitative ratings and qualitative comments from 50 professionals in counseling, psychology, student mental health, education, and related helping professions, followed by target-user evaluation involving 300 first-year students who met the screening criterion for elevated depressive symptoms. Professional ratings indicated satisfactory content adequacy (overall mean item score = 3.496; S-CVI/Ave = 0.951). Student ratings were also favorable (overall M = 4.112), particularly for clarity, organization, and usability. Integrated findings supported the guide’s formative value while identifying needs for more concrete examples, first-year life scenarios, accessible delivery formats, and clearer help-seeking guidance.

items.title: Sports+Empowering Rural Revitalization: Research on the Living Inheritance of Yunnan Ethnic Traditional Sports and Rural Spatial Production: A Spatial Production Theory Perspective
items.source: Academic journal of management and social sciences

extra.summary: China's rural revitalization policy has put sport to work as a development tool, but we still know surprisingly little about what sport actually does to the places where it is used. This paper looks at Yunnan, where ethnic minority communities have practiced traditional sports for generations, and asks how these practices shape the production of rural space. items.title: Digital Competence Development for Information Engineering Students in Higher Education Institutions in Yunnan Province: A Research Framework and Preliminary Exploration
items.affiliation: Kunming University of Science and Technology; Srinakharinwirot University

extra.summary: With the deepening of global digital transformation and the advancement of China's "Digital Yunnan" strategy, digital competence has become a core competency for information engineering students to adapt to industrial upgrading and national development needs. This study examines digital competence development in four higher education institutions in Yunnan Province through a diagnostic survey, expert consultation, and a single-group pretest-posttest intervention. The diagnostic survey retained 413 valid responses from institutions with a combined information engineering enrollment of 5,621. The framework integrates Digital Awareness, Digital Knowledge, Digital Skills, Digital Security, and Digital Ethics and connects these dimensions to international frameworks and engineering education. Following an eight-session, 24-hour program, 30 students at Kunming University of Science and Technology reported higher overall competence at posttest (M = 3.52, SD = 0.41) than at pretest (M = 3.01, SD = 0.46), t(29) = 8.716, p < .001. Digital Security and Digital Skills showed the largest reported relative gains. These findings provide preliminary evidence of change following the program. The absence of a comparison group and delayed assessment limits causal interpretation, evidence of retention, and generalization beyond the participating institutions.

extra.summary: Ethnic traditional sports constitute a distinctive vehicle for cultural transmission and physical activity among ethnic minority youth, yet their psychological correlates remain underexplored. items.title: Between Humanism and Market Naturalism
items.source: Erasmus Journal for Philosophy and Economics

extra.summary: On the 250th anniversary of The Wealth of Nations, this article revisits Adam Smith’s legacy by examining his reception in Karl Polanyi’s The Great Transformation. While Polanyi sharply criticizes Smith for contributing to the naturalization of market exchange, he simultaneously presents Smith as a thinker whose political economy rests on humanistic foundations. The article reconstructs this apparent tension by critically examining Polanyi’s reception of Smith’s anthropology, theory of the division of labour, and conception of wealth. It argues that Polanyi offers a largely convincing account of Smith’s rejection of economic naturalism, while misreading Smith’s account of human motivation. The paper concludes that Smith is understood as a transitional figure: the founder of political economy whose thought remains subordinate to social purposes and therefore cannot alone ground the idea of a fully self-regulating market. This interpretation contributes to contemporary philosophical debates on market society and economic embeddedness.

items.title: Cosmic Sensibility for Cosmopolitics: Making Sense in the Anthropocene
items.affiliation: Lithuanian Academy of Music and Theatre

extra.summary: In response to Philippe Descola’s call for a cosmopolitics adequate to the crisis of the multiscalar Anthropocene, this paper interrogates the problem of entangled coexistence by shifting the analytical register to sensibility. The paper therefore proposes the speculative concept of cosmic sensibility, which mobilizes sense as constitutive of cosmopolitics and names a relational openness through which distinct entities become mutually sense-able without necessarily presupposing their commensurability. The concept synthesizes insights from the ontological turn (Descola, Viveiros de Castro, Hui), process-relational cosmology (Whitehead) and cosmopolitics (Stengers), as well as feminist STS (Barad, Haraway), in order to sketch its provisional contours across three interconnected registers: onto-epistemological, cosmopolitical, and ethical. Reading in parallel a line of authors who rethink the anthropocentric assumptions of the cosmos in relational terms, the paper contends that ontological plurality becomes cosmopolitically consequential only insofar as agents inhabiting heterogeneous worlds can enter into relations of mutual sense-ability. Cosmic sensibility thus reframes entangled coexistence as a practice of dwelling halfway, sustaining difference while remaining response-able to the worldings produced through the encounter.
